opus-5.5.text:
Scaling has been one of the most reliable levers we've had, and I don't think anyone who's worked on these models would deny that. When you increase model capacity, train on more data, and spend more compute, you consistently see improvements: better prompt adherence, more coherent compositions, better handling of things that used to be notoriously hard, like text rendering, hands, or counting objects correctly. A lot of capabilities that people assumed would need special architectural tricks just emerged once the models got big enough.

That said, I'd push back a little on the idea that scaling is the whole story. Image generation is different from language in some important ways. For one, the data question matters enormously. It's not just how many images you have, it's the quality of the images and especially the quality of the captions. Some of the biggest jumps we've seen came from better text-image alignment, like recaptioning datasets with much more detailed, accurate descriptions, rather than just adding more raw pairs scraped from the web. So I think of data quality as its own scaling axis, and in some ways a more important one.

Second, there's the question of what you're optimizing for. With images, the final judge is often human aesthetic preference, which is subtle and somewhat subjective. You can scale a model and get something that's technically more capable but not necessarily more pleasing or more useful to a creative professional. That's where post-training, preference tuning, and careful evaluation come in, and those don't automatically get solved by making the model bigger.

And third, there's efficiency. Image and especially video generation are expensive at inference time, so if the only path forward is "make it bigger," you run into real practical limits on who can use these tools and how interactive they can be. I find a lot of the most interesting work right now is in getting the benefits of scale while making sampling faster, through distillation, better architectures, and smarter latent representations.

So my view is that scaling is necessary, and it's given us a remarkable foundation, but the differentiation increasingly comes from everything around it: the data, the alignment with what people actually want, controllability, and making these models practical enough to fit into real creative workflows.

r001.rationale: The candidate says scaling consistently improves image models, but it does not identify whether those improvements continue at sizes comparable to language models as an unresolved question.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. When I think about scaling for image generation, I actually try to separate out a few different axes, because people often lump them together.

The first is scaling the model itself, the parameter count. And honestly, image models have been comparatively small for a long time. Stable Diffusion at launch was under a billion parameters, which is tiny next to what was happening in language at the same time. So there's been a lot of headroom there, and when you push the capacity up, you do see the model get better at composition, at following complicated prompts, at rendering text, at the things that require a kind of "understanding" of the scene rather than just texture synthesis.

The second axis is data, and I'd argue this matters more in images than people appreciate. Scaling data isn't just about more images, it's about better paired data. A huge amount of the progress in the last couple of years came from improving the captions, either by recaptioning datasets with vision-language models or by being much more careful about what you train on. A model trained on billions of noisy alt-text pairs learns a lot of wrong associations. So "scaling" here is partly scaling quality, not just volume.

The third axis is compute, and in particular inference compute. This is the one I find most interesting right now. In language we've seen that letting the model think longer at test time can substitute for a larger model. Images have an analogous story: more sampling steps, better guidance, iterative refinement, or having a model critique and redraw its own output. You can trade off training-time scale for inference-time scale, and for a lot of applications that's the right trade.

The thing I'd caution against is assuming the scaling laws transfer directly from text. The evaluation problem is much harder for images. Perplexity gives you a clean curve in language; for images, FID and CLIP scores are only loosely correlated with what a person actually thinks looks good or correct. So you can scale and watch your metrics improve while real users don't notice, or vice versa. That means a lot of the practical work is about figuring out what you're actually scaling toward.

And finally, scaling alone doesn't solve everything. Spatial reasoning, counting, precise control, consistency across multiple images, these improve with scale but they don't get solved by scale. You still need architectural ideas and better conditioning. So I see scaling as the baseline you have to get right, but the interesting research is in what you do on top of it.

r001.rationale: The response says image models have had headroom and that increasing capacity improves several capabilities. It does not identify as unresolved whether image-generation models continue improving when scaled to sizes comparable to language models.

astra-6.text:
I think scaling is a very powerful way to improve image generation, but it’s worth unpacking what we mean by scaling. There’s model size, there’s the amount of training data, and there’s the compute you put into training. Those things have to work together. Just making a model bigger doesn’t necessarily help if the data doesn’t support it.

What’s exciting is that, as you scale, you can get improvements beyond visual quality. The model can become better at following a prompt and capturing relationships between objects. You might have a model that makes a beautiful image, but it doesn’t actually depict what you asked for. That’s a different dimension of progress.

The challenge is figuring out what’s still limiting you. Is it capacity? Is it data quality or the descriptions paired with the images? Or is it something about the training objective? I see scaling as an important ingredient, but you still need to understand those bottlenecks to make good use of it.

r001.rationale: The response says scaling can improve image generation, but it does not identify whether scaling to language-model-comparable sizes continues to help as an unresolved question.

sol-6.1.text:
I think scaling is a really powerful tool for image generation, but there are a few dimensions to it. You can scale the model, you can scale the amount of training data, and you can scale the compute you spend training it. Those things need to work together. A larger model gives you more capacity, but you still need data that teaches it the relationships you want it to learn.

And image quality is only part of the story. You also want the model to follow the prompt—to get the objects, their attributes, and the relationships between them right. You can have an image that looks beautiful but doesn't actually depict what you asked for. So the question is not just whether scaling makes images look better, but whether it makes the model more reliable and controllable.

I see scaling as a very strong foundation. But the data, the training objective, and how we evaluate the results still matter a lot.

r001.rationale: The response describes scaling as powerful but does not identify continued improvement at language-model-comparable sizes as an unresolved question.
